\begin{proof}
Let
\[
I=\int_0^1\log(\sin \pi x)\,dx.
\]
Using \(\sin(\pi x)=\sin(\pi(1-x))\), we also have
\[
I=\int_0^1\log(\sin \pi(1-x))\,dx.
\]
Therefore,
\[
2I=\int_0^1\log\bigl(\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi(1-x))\bigr)\,dx
=\int_0^1\log(\sin^2(\pi x))\,dx.
\]
Since \(\sin(\pi x)>0\) for \(0<x<1\), this equals
\[
2I=2\int_0^1\log(\sin \pi x)\,dx,
\]
which alone is tautological. Instead, apply \(x\mapsto x/2\) and use \(\sin(2t)=2\sin t\cos t\):
\[
I=\int_0^1\log(\sin \pi x)\,dx
=\int_0^1\log(2\sin(\pi x/2)\cos(\pi x/2))\,dx.
\]
The substitutions \(u=x/2\) and \(u=(1-x)/2\) give
\[
I=\log 2+\int_0^1\log(\sin(\pi u))\,du-\log 2-I.
\]
Thus \(2I=-2\log 2\), and hence \(I=-\log 2\).\n\end{proof}

\]
The integral converges because \(\log(\sin \pi x)\sim\log(\pi x)\) near \(0\) and similarly near \(1\). With \(t=\pi x\),

\]
By symmetry of sine,
\[
I=\frac2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\sin t)\,dt.
\]
Let \(J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\sin t)\,dt\). Substituting \(t\mapsto \pi/2-t\) yields
\[
J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\cos t)\,dt.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\sin t\cos t)\,dt
=\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\left(\frac12\sin(2t)\right)dt.
\]
Thus
\[
2J=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2+\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\sin 2t)\,dt.
\]
Using \(u=2t\), the remaining integral is \(\frac12\int_0^\pi\log(\sin u)du=J\). Hence \(J=-\frac\pi2\log 2\), and therefore
\[
I=\frac2\pi J=-\log 2.
\]
\end{proof}
